items.title: The oxygen you breathe comes from WATER, not CO2
items.claim: Photosynthesis takes in CO2 and water and produces sugar and oxygen. Every chemistry student writes the equation. But the O2 released is not stripped from the CO2 — it comes entirely from splitting water molecules.
items.prompt: How do we know the oxygen comes from water?

options.text: Both water and CO2 contribute oxygen equally
Ruben and Kamen (1941) used the heavy isotope oxygen-18 to label either water or CO2; the released O2 carried the label only when the water was labelled, never when the CO2 was
CO2 is the source of the oxygen

items.reveal:
The light reactions of photosynthesis split water (photolysis) at the oxygen-evolving complex — a manganese-calcium cluster in Photosystem II. Two water molecules are split: 2 H2O -> 4 H+ + 4 e- + O2.

The electrons enter the electron transport chain. The protons contribute to the thylakoid pH gradient (lumen reaches pH ~5, stroma ~8). ATP synthase uses the gradient to make ATP.

The Calvin cycle (in the stroma) uses ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar. The carbon from CO2 becomes the carbon in glucose. But the oxygen atoms in CO2 mostly end up in carbohydrate, NOT in the released O2.

Oxygen is, from photosynthesis's point of view, a waste product — and arguably the most consequential pollution event in Earth's history (the Great Oxidation Event, ~2.4 billion years ago, killed most anaerobic life).
items.why: The arrow-pushing equation suggests CO2 donates oxygen. The actual chemistry inverts that: water is split, CO2 is reduced, and the oxygen you breathe was once dissolved in a chloroplast.

items.title: You convert nitrogen waste into your own pee chemistry every day
items.claim: Breaking down amino acids releases ammonia (NH3) — toxic to cells at concentrations above ~50 micromolar. Mammals convert it to urea, a relatively harmless molecule that can be safely concentrated and excreted in urine. Fish dump ammonia directly into water; birds convert it to uric acid.
items.prompt: Why do different animals handle nitrogen waste differently?

options.text: Water availability drives the choice: fish (ammoniotelic, ammonia) need lots of water for dilution; mammals (ureotelic, urea) use moderate water; birds and reptiles (uricotelic, uric acid) save water by making a near-solid waste — important for desert and egg-laying animals

items.reveal:
Ammonia (NH3): produced by deamination of amino acids. Toxic at low concentrations. Fish, most aquatic invertebrates excrete it directly through gills — the surrounding water dilutes it.

Urea: synthesised by the urea cycle in the liver (Krebs and Henseleit, 1932 — the same Hans Krebs who later won the Nobel for the citric acid cycle). Five reactions, costs 4 ATP per urea. Each urea carries 2 nitrogen atoms. Soluble, moderately concentrated in urine (up to ~50x blood concentration in humans).

Uric acid: birds, reptiles, insects. Synthesis costs even more energy than urea (~10 ATP per nitrogen handled) but precipitates as semi-solid pellets, requiring almost no water for excretion. The white component of bird droppings is uric acid.

Note: egg-laying animals (birds, reptiles, monotremes) need a non-toxic, water-poor waste form that won't poison the developing embryo. Uric acid fits the niche.

In humans, uric acid is a byproduct of nucleic acid breakdown (not protein). Gout is precipitation of uric acid crystals in joints.

Marine mammals (whales, seals) face the opposite challenge: no fresh water for dilution. They use highly concentrated urine instead.
items.why: Waste seems like a non-design decision. The form of nitrogen excretion is one of evolution's deepest trade-offs — tying physiology, water economy and even reproductive biology together.

items.title: A mouse uses more energy per gram than an elephant
items.claim: Kleiber's law: metabolic rate scales as body mass to the 3/4 power. Bigger animals have lower metabolic rate per unit mass. A mouse uses ~50x more calories per gram per day than an elephant.
items.prompt: Why scaling exponent of 3/4 and not 1 or 2/3?

options.text: Surface-area scaling (2/3) would predict heat loss only. The 3/4 exponent reflects the geometry of branching vascular and respiratory networks delivering resources to cells (West, Brown, Enquist 1997)
Because heart rate scales as mass
All animals have the same metabolic rate

items.reveal:
Max Kleiber (1932): metabolic rate (B) scales as body mass (M) to the 3/4. B = a * M^0.75. Holds from mice to elephants over six orders of magnitude.

Consequences:
- Mass-specific rate (B/M) scales as M^(-1/4). A 30 gram mouse uses ~50x more O2 per gram than a 3000 kg elephant.
- Heart rate scales as M^(-1/4). Mice: ~600 bpm; humans: ~70 bpm; elephants: ~30 bpm; blue whales: ~10 bpm.
- Lifespan scales as M^(1/4). Mice live 2-3 years; humans 80; whales 100+.
- Total heartbeats per lifetime are roughly constant (~1-2 billion) across mammals (with humans as an outlier — we get more).

The 3/4 exponent puzzled biologists for decades. West, Brown and Enquist (1997, Science) proposed it falls out of optimal branching transport networks (vascular trees, lungs). The model fits remarkably well across taxa.

Applications: drug dosing across species (allometric scaling guides initial doses); ecological energetics (predicting how many predators a habitat can support); aging research (the 'rate of living' hypothesis links metabolism to lifespan).
items.why: Per-gram metabolic rate is highly NOT constant across animals. Body size determines life pace — fast or slow — through physical constraints on how internal transport networks scale.
